To facilitate the comparisons of the nighttime crash frequencies in the two cities, the project team calculated a dimming effect (DE) for the after LED conversion period and a pseudo dimming effect (DE ) for the before LED conversion period. Based on the two models developed P for the after period, the DE was calculated as the expected ND crash ratio between the two cities as following: (1) 𝐸𝐸(𝑁𝑁𝐶𝐶)/𝐸𝐸(𝐷𝐷𝐶𝐶) 𝐷𝐷w𝐷𝐷he=re: 𝐸𝐸(𝑁𝑁𝑆𝑆)/𝐸𝐸(𝐷𝐷𝑆𝑆) DE = adaptive lighting system dimming effect on crashes; E(Nc) = expected nighttime frequency for Cambridge after the LED conversion; E(Dc) = expected daytime frequency for Cambridge after the LED conversion; E(Ns) = expected nighttime frequency for Somerville after the LED conversion; and E(Ds) = expected daytime frequency for Somerville after the LED conversion. Note that, although negative binomial regression has been widely accepted as a robust method for modeling crash data, considering the inherent limitations of statistical modeling methods and missing roadway, traffic, and driver population information, the pseudo dimming effect, which was computed following the same method based on the two before-period models, was used for comparison with the DE determined based on the after-period models. Table 24 summarizes the parameter estimates of the four models for the adaptive lighting indicator, followed by Table 28 comparing the dimming effects before and after the LED conversion. The after models showed a nighttime crash increase of approximately 30% for C1 roadways in Cambridge after midnight with the dimmed lighting levels. The pseudo dimming effect for the before LED conversion period was, however, estimated to be close to 1 (i.e., 1.02).
